name: Black Death in Florence and Italy
summary: The Black Death reached Italian ports from the Crimea in late 1347 and spread through the peninsula with devastating speed. Florence lost roughly 50,000–60,000 of its pre-plague population of perhaps 100,000 in 1348. Giovanni Boccaccio, an eyewitness, opened the Decameron with a vivid account of the city's collapse. The catastrophe fundamentally altered the Italian economy, art, and collective psychology.
outcomes: Florence loses roughly half its population
Boccaccio witnesses and records the disaster
Labor shortages empower surviving peasants and artisans

_quarry.structural_significance: Italy's unique position as a densely urbanized, trade-connected region made it one of the worst-affected areas; the social and economic disruption accelerated the shifts that produced the Renaissance.

sources_used: Herlihy, The Black Death and the Transformation of the West
